newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch swine fever toll worsens, pork prices rise.
newsitem.headline: Dutch swine fever toll worsens, pork prices rise.

text.p: Two more cases of swine fever surfaced in the Netherlands on Tuesday, and the leading retailer said it had had no option but to raise pork prices in the shops.

The Dutch Farm Ministry said the disease had now been detected at two new farms, taking the total affected to 133, 12 more than a week ago. Around one million pigs have so far been destroyed in a bid to control the disease, which although highly contagious to pigs, is not harmful to humans.

The leading Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn said it had been forced to raise its prices for pork this week by one guilder a kilo in response to a meat shortage, which has sent wholesale market prices to all-time highs.
"We have had to take the step because the prices we have to pay have gone up so much," a spokesman said.
The price Dutch slaughterhouses pay for live pigs have topped five guilders a kilo for the first time ever. At the start of the year, the pigs were fetching just three guilders.
And retailers admitted there were more rises to come.
"This will certainly not be the last price increase we see in the near future. We haven't reached the top yet," the Albert Heijn spokesman said.
The government has imposed strict controls on the pig sector in a bid to stamp out the disease, first discovered in February and the first to hit the country for five years.
Its efforts have included imposing a transport ban on livestock, manure and semen in almost half the country and strict checks on all pig farms nationwide.

So big is the task that the army has had to be called in to help with the transportation of animals to slaughterhouses and the cost to the farming industry is believed to be running close to one billion guilders.

The Netherlands has lost key export revenue because of the disease, which led the European Union to impose a ban on Dutch pig exports and many countries including the United States to extend the ban to imports of Dutch pork products.
Pig and pork exports were worth more than five billion guilders to the Netherlands last year.
According to a report from the U.S. embassy in The Hague this week, Dutch exports of live pigs would be cut by half this year, possibly opening up a new market for U.S. exporters.

"The hog cholera (swine fever) crisis theoretically provides the opportunity for the United States to export live pigs to the European Union," the report said. However, it added that meeting strict EU import requirements, such as whole herd testing, would probably make such a move prohibitive ona cost basis.

"Because new cases continue to occur regularly, there is not a lot of optimism the hog cholera crisis will be over soon," the report said, adding the EU export and internal tranport ban were expected to be remain place for several months.
